title: Number of Islands
description: DFS flood fill: every unvisited "1" starts a new island; sink it by overwriting connected land with "0". O(rows*cols).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I get a 2D grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), and I count the number of islands — where an island is a maximal group of land cells connected 4-directionally (up/down/left/right, not diagonals)."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Cell type — are these the strings '1'/'0' or the numbers 1/0? (LeetCode uses strings; matters for the equality check.)
• Connectivity — 4-directional or 8-directional? (Default is 4.)
• Can I mutate the input grid, or do I need a separate visited set?
• Edges — does land at the border count as bordered by water, or is the border itself water? (Standard interpretation: anything off-grid is water.)
• Empty grid — return 0?
sections.why: The string-vs-number question is the load-bearing one — if you compare with `=== 1` when the cell is `'1'`, your DFS never enters and you return 0. The mutation question matters because the cleanest solution sinks visited land in-place, which destroys the input — if mutation is forbidden, you need an O(R*C) visited matrix instead. Asking up front is cheaper than rewriting halfway through.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious approach before optimizing.
sections.say: "The brute force is basically the same algorithm — there's no O(n²) version that's meaningfully different. Every land cell has to be visited at least once just to confirm it's part of an island, so the floor is O(R*C). The naive thing would be to use Union-Find: walk every cell, and for each '1' union it with each of its 4 '1' neighbors. At the end, count distinct roots. That works and gives O(R*C*α(R*C)), but it's more bookkeeping than necessary — DFS flood fill is the same asymptotic with a tiny constant."
sections.why: This problem is unusual in that the brute force IS the optimal — there's no factor-of-n improvement to discover. The right move is to name an alternative algorithm (Union-Find) and explain why DFS wins on simplicity, rather than inventing a strawman O(R²C²) just so you have something to optimize away. Interviewers respect knowing when a problem doesn't have a clever speedup.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to grid-DFS flood fill?
sections.say: "This is the canonical 'matrix as implicit graph' problem. Each '1' cell is a node; its 4-neighbors that are also '1' are its edges — but we never materialize an adjacency list, we just compute neighbors on the fly with (r±1, c) and (r, c±1). Counting islands is counting connected components in that implicit graph, which is the textbook DFS-from-each-unvisited-node pattern. The flood-fill twist is that we mark cells visited by sinking them to '0' in place — that doubles as 'visited' and saves the O(R*C) auxiliary set. The outer double loop scans every cell exactly once; the inner DFS sinks one whole component, so each cell is touched at most twice total (once by the outer scan, once by a DFS)."
sections.why: Naming the pattern AND the structural property is the move. 'It's a DFS problem' is a guess; 'matrix is an implicit graph where 4-neighbors are edges, and connected components on that graph is exactly islands' is a derivation. The in-place sinking trick is the specific implementation insight that separates this from a generic DFS — call it out because the alternative (visited matrix) is correct but uses 2x memory and an extra parameter to thread through.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a multi-island grid with a diagonal-touching pair (which must NOT merge), an all-water case, and one big island shaped to verify the flood fills around its hole.

examples.note: Classic case — three distinct islands. Note (2,2) and (3,3) touch only diagonally → still separate islands under 4-connectivity.
examples.trace:
outer scan (0,0)='1' → count=1, dfs sinks (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) → top-left 2x2 all become '0'
outer scan (0,1)='0', (0,2)..(0,4)='0', (1,0)..(1,4)='0' → all already sunk or water
outer scan (2,2)='1' → count=2, dfs sinks (2,2) — neighbors are all '0' or off-grid
outer scan (3,3)='1' → count=3, dfs sinks (3,3) and (3,4)
outer scan finishes → return 3

examples.note: Degenerate all-water — outer loop visits every cell but the `if (grid[r][c] === '1')` guard never fires.
examples.trace:
outer scan (0,0)='0' → skip
outer scan (0,1)='0' → skip
outer scan (1,0)='0' → skip
outer scan (1,1)='0' → skip
return count=0 (never incremented)

examples.note: Plus-shape — confirms the flood follows 4-connectivity around the two water cells without splitting.
examples.trace:
outer scan (0,0)='1' → count=1, launch dfs
  dfs floods (0,0)→(0,1)→(0,2), backtracks via (0,1)→(1,1)→(2,1)→(2,0) and (2,2)
  all eight land cells sink to '0'
outer scan continues — every remaining cell is '0', no more islands
return count=1

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the one bug this problem keeps catching: the string-vs-number mismatch. If you write `grid[r][c] === 1` instead of `=== '1'`, the trace immediately shows the outer scan never finding any land and returning 0. The plus-shape example also defends 4-connectivity — if you accidentally added diagonals (5 or 8 neighbor calls), the trace wouldn't change for this case, but it would over-merge the first example's (2,2) and (1,1) into one island. Worth picking an example that distinguishes.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty grid `[]` → `grid[0]` throws. Guard with `if (!grid.length || !grid[0].length) return 0` at the top.
• Single cell — `[['1']]` returns 1, `[['0']]` returns 0. The double loop handles both without special cases.
• All land — one big island, returns 1. DFS visits every cell exactly once.
• All water — returns 0, the if-guard never fires.
• Single row or single column — works, but worth tracing once because the recursion is now strictly linear.
• Diagonal-only adjacency (e.g. two '1's at (0,0) and (1,1) surrounded by water) → must NOT merge under 4-connectivity; returns 2. This is the bug a sloppy 8-direction loop would create.
• Very large grid — recursion depth can hit O(R*C) on a snake-shaped island, which blows the JS stack around 10k-15k cells. For interview purposes I'd flag this and offer an iterative-stack variant as the fallback."
sections.why: The empty-grid guard is the cheap one most candidates forget — `grid[0].length` throws on `[]`. The diagonal-adjacency call-out shows you read the connectivity rule carefully rather than assuming. The recursion-depth concern is the senior move: most candidates ship the recursive version without thinking about stack limits, and on a 200x200 grid filled with a single snaky island that's an actual bug. Naming it and offering the iterative-stack alternative is the right level of paranoia.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(R*C). Two passes maximum over each cell: once by the outer double loop, and once by a DFS that sinks it. The outer loop touches every cell in O(R*C); each DFS visit is O(1) work (bounds check, equality check, four recursive calls). The total DFS work across all components sums to O(R*C) because each land cell is sunk exactly once and water cells are bailed on immediately.

Space is O(R*C) worst case — the recursion stack for a single snake-shaped island that fills the whole grid. If we used the iterative-stack version, it's still O(R*C) for the stack but no actual recursion frames. Sinking in place is what saves us the O(R*C) visited matrix.

If you wanted to extend to 'count islands in a STREAM of land additions' (LeetCode 305, Number of Islands II), the DFS approach doesn't work — adding a single land cell could merge up to 4 existing islands. That's Union-Find's home turf: each add does up-to-4 union operations, total O(K*α(R*C)) for K additions. Same template I mentioned in section 2, just used in a regime where it actually wins."
sections.why: The two-passes-per-cell argument is the clean amortization defense — interviewers sometimes ask 'isn't the DFS itself O(R*C) per call, and you call it from inside a loop, so isn't it O((R*C)²)?' The answer is no, because once a cell is sunk it'll never be visited again. The streaming-additions extension is the killer follow-up: it's LeetCode 305, it explicitly motivates Union-Find as the better tool for that regime, and it proves you see the problem family, not just this instance. That's how the same pattern shows up in Surrounded Regions, Max Area of Island, and Walls and Gates.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the DFS flood-fill on a real grid. The trace simulates the recursion with an explicit stack so you can see each sink and how the count only bumps when a fresh '1' is found in the outer scan.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter numIslands — ${rows}x${cols} grid`, state: { grid: grid.map(r => r.join('')) } };
yield { line: 2, label: `rows=${rows}, cols=${cols}`, state: { grid: grid.map(r => r.join('')), rows, cols } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init count=0', state: { grid: grid.map(r => r.join('')), count } };
yield { line: 14, label: `outer scan (${r},${c}) — grid[${r}][${c}]='${grid[r][c]}'`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count, r, c } };
yield { line: 14, label: `found land — count → ${count}, launch dfs(${r},${c})`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count, r, c } };
if (cr < 0 || cr >= rows || cc < 0 || cc >= cols || grid[cr][cc] !== '1') {
yield { line: 5, label: `dfs(${cr},${cc}) — out-of-bounds or not '1', return`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count, current: [cr, cc], stackSize: stack.length } };
yield { line: 6, label: `sink (${cr},${cc}) → '0'`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count, current: [cr, cc], stackSize: stack.length } };
yield { line: 10, label: `enqueue 4 neighbors of (${cr},${cc})`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count, current: [cr, cc], stackSize: stack.length } };
yield { line: 11, label: `dfs finished — island ${count} fully sunk`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count } };
yield { line: 18, label: `return ${count}`, state: { grid: grid.map(rw => rw.join('')), count, returns: count } };

notes: Sink cells to "0" in-place to avoid a separate visited set — but it MUTATES the input.
Bounds check FIRST inside dfs; that lets you call neighbors blindly without per-call guards.
Grid cells are strings ("1"/"0"), not numbers — compare with the matching type.

alternates.label: BFS flood-fill (iterative queue)
alternates.when: Reach for BFS when you want to avoid recursion-stack overflow on large grids (a snake-shaped island of 200x200 would blow the JS call stack with DFS). BFS uses an explicit queue of bounded size so depth is not an issue.
notes: Sink each cell to '0' BEFORE pushing it to the queue — prevents the same cell from being enqueued multiple times by different neighbors.
BFS and DFS produce the same island count; BFS visits the component level-by-level rather than depth-first.
O(R*C) queue space in the worst case (a solid land rectangle); trade recursion depth for queue width.

alternates.label: Union-Find (non-mutating)
alternates.when: Use Union-Find when you must NOT mutate the input grid or when the problem asks 'given streaming land additions, report the island count after each one' (LeetCode 305). For a static grid DFS is simpler; UF shines for dynamic connectivity.
notes: Initialize count to the number of land cells; each union of two distinct roots merges two islands, so count decrements once.
Flatten the 2D index to 1D via r*cols+c so the parent array is a plain 1D array.
Only check right and down neighbors (not left/up) to process each edge once — correctness preserved since union is symmetric.

questions.q: What does sinking a visited cell to "0" accomplish?
options: Saves memory vs. a separate visited set
Prevents revisits that would re-count the same island
Both
Neither
O(R+C)
O(R*C)
O(log(R*C))

questions.q: Why bounds-check at the TOP of dfs?
options: It runs the four equality comparisons in one place, which V8 hoists out of the loop
So recursive calls can be made blindly without per-neighbor checks
Avoids stack overflow by short-circuiting before the recursive calls allocate frames
Ensures the sink-to-'0' write happens before any neighbor reads the cell
Up, down, left, right
All 8 including diagonals
Knight-move offsets (the L-shaped chess pattern)
Up and right only (the upper-right quadrant)

questions.q: Counting islands is really which classic graph task on the grid-as-implicit-graph?
options: Topological sort
Counting connected components
Shortest path
Detecting a directed cycle
questions.explain: Each '1' is a node and same-value 4-neighbors are edges; the number of islands is exactly the number of connected components.

questions.q: Why is topological sort the WRONG tool for this problem?
options: Topo sort processes nodes level-by-level, which would split a single island across multiple BFS layers
The grid graph is undirected and has no ordering/dependency to sort
Topo sort can only count components in DAGs; grid graphs always contain 4-cycles around water cells
Kahn's algorithm requires a zero-indegree node to seed, but every land cell starts with indegree > 0
questions.explain: Topo sort orders a directed acyclic graph by dependencies; islands are about undirected connectivity, where there is no edge direction to order.

questions.q: If you removed the visited-marking (never sinking cells to '0'), what happens?
options: Still correct on grids that have no 2x2 land blocks, because no cycle can form on a single row
DFS revisits land it already entered and recurses forever (infinite loop)
Correct count but each island's interior cells are counted multiple times in the outer loop
Returns 1 for any grid containing land, because every connected component merges into one
questions.explain: Two adjacent land cells point at each other, so without marking visited the DFS bounces between them endlessly.

questions.q: Union-Find is the better tool than DFS flood-fill when:
options: The grid is very large
Land cells are added one-at-a-time and you must report the island count after each add (dynamic connectivity)
There are diagonal connections
You only need a boolean answer
questions.explain: For a static grid DFS and Union-Find are both O(R*C); Union-Find wins on streaming additions (LeetCode 305) where each new cell may merge up to 4 existing islands.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the DFS flood-fill island counter.

L3.prompt: Write `numIslands(grid)` (grid is char[][] of "1"/"0"). Use DFS flood fill. Log the result for a 4x5 grid with three islands.
hints: Outer double loop finds new "1" cells; each starts an island.
DFS sinks all connected land to "0" so it is not recounted.
Bounds check at the top of dfs lets you recurse blindly into 4 neighbors.
